item.title: Funazushi: Japan's Oldest Sushi, Fermented on Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Funazushi is the ancestor of all sushi: nigorobuna carp from Lake Biwa, salted and then buried in cooked rice to ferment for one to three years, a preservation method over a millennium old from which modern sushi eventually evolved. The result is nothing like the sushi the world knows — the flesh turns dense, tangy and creamy, with an aroma often compared to strong cheese — and it remains a proud, polarising delicacy cured by family houses around the lake, served sliced with the golden fermented rice, floated in hot broth as ochazuke, or nibbled alongside local sake, which flatters it best.

item.title: Shiga Food Guide: Omi Beef, Funazushi, and Lake Biwa Cuisine
item.description: Shiga Prefecture’s food identity is shaped almost entirely by Lake Biwa. The lake provides a suite of endemic freshwater fish that appear nowhere else on Japanese menus, and the pastures and rice paddies of the surrounding basin have nurtured Japan’s oldest named wagyu beef tradition. Eating well in Shiga means understanding these local ingredients — and being willing to venture beyond the expected. Omi Beef — Japan’s Oldest Wagyu Brand Most visitors know Kobe beef.
